title: DID JESUS ACCEPT EVERYONE—OR DID HE CALL EVERYONE TO REPENT? THE ANSWER MAY SHATTER WHAT YOU THOUGHT YOU KNEW ABOUT HIS LOVE.
paragraphs: DID JESUS ACCEPT EVERYONE—OR DID HE CALL EVERYONE TO REPENT? THE ANSWER MAY SHATTER WHAT YOU THOUGHT YOU KNEW ABOUT HIS LOVE.

He welcomed the people religion rejected. He confronted the sins people defended. And He loved sinners too deeply to leave them unchanged. Somewhere between “Jesus accepts me as I am” and “Jesus demands that I change,” we have forgotten the breathtaking, uncomfortable, life-changing truth of the Gospel.
There was a woman standing in front of Jesus who had every reason to be terrified.
Her shame was public.
Her sin had been exposed.

The people surrounding her were not interested in her restoration. They wanted a verdict. They wanted punishment. They wanted to see what Jesus would do when confronted with someone whose wrongdoing could no longer be hidden.
And there she stood.
No defense.
No escape.
No way to rewrite what had happened.
Then Jesus spoke.
And the stones never fell.
But what happened next is the part of the story our generation desperately needs to hear.
Jesus did not simply say, “You are accepted. Go live however you want.”
He said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Mercy.
And a command to leave sin behind.
Grace.
And a call to a different life.
The same Jesus who refused to condemn her also refused to celebrate the sin that had brought her there.

And before we go any further, there is something important we must acknowledge about this passage. The account of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) is absent from many of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John, and its original placement in the New Testament is disputed. It has been treasured throughout Christian history, but we should not build an entire doctrine on a text whose manuscript history requires such honesty.
Thankfully, the truth illustrated by this account is firmly established in passages whose textual standing is not similarly disputed.
Jesus welcomed sinners.
Jesus called sinners to repentance.
And He never treated those two realities as enemies.
Now here is the question that might be harder to answer than we expect.
What if the Jesus we have been defending is not always the Jesus the Scriptures actually reveal?
What if some of us have turned His grace into permission to remain unchanged?
And what if others have turned His holiness into a weapon against the very people He came to save?
Because the real Jesus will confront both.
And perhaps that is why we sometimes find Him so uncomfortable.
We want a Savior who understands our pain.
But do we want a Lord who challenges our choices?
We want forgiveness for what we have done.
But do we want freedom from what keeps pulling us back?
We want Him to welcome us at our worst.
But are we willing to let Him transform what we have learned to defend?
These are not questions for the people we dislike.
They are questions for us.
For the person reading this while quietly fighting an addiction nobody knows about.
For the believer who worships on Sunday and struggles with the same secret sin on Monday.
For the Christian who has become so skilled at identifying other people's sins that they have stopped noticing their own pride.
For the person who has been wounded by a church and wonders whether Jesus would reject them too.
For the exhausted soul who has promised God a hundred times that things would change, only to find themselves crying over the same failure again.
And for the person who has mistaken God's patience for His approval.
Jesus has something to say to every one of us.
But first, we must listen to what He actually said.
When Jesus began His public ministry in Galilee, Mark recorded His proclamation:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
In the original Greek, two words deserve our attention.
μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) — repent.
πιστεύετε (pisteuete) — believe.
These are present imperative forms, calling Jesus' hearers to respond to the arrival of God's kingdom.
The Greek verb metanoeō, from which metanoeite comes, speaks of repentance—a change of mind and orientation that, in biblical context, involves turning from sin toward God.
It is more than momentary regret.
It is more than feeling ashamed after getting caught.
It is more than crying during worship and returning deliberately to the same rebellion without any desire to change.
Biblical repentance involves a genuine turning toward God, expressed in a changed direction of life.
And pisteuete calls people to believe the good news—to trust the Gospel Jesus proclaimed.
Notice something remarkable.
Jesus did not announce the kingdom of God by telling people they had to make themselves perfect before approaching Him.
But neither did He announce that repentance was unnecessary.
He proclaimed repentance and faith together.
The Gospel is not that you can earn God's love by becoming good enough.
The Gospel is that God's grace reaches sinners who cannot save themselves, calls them to turn to Him, and begins transforming them through Jesus Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
Because somewhere along the way, we have allowed the word acceptance to carry meanings that Jesus never gave it.
We have confused being welcomed with being affirmed in everything we do.
We have confused compassion with moral agreement.
We have confused forgiveness with the absence of consequences.
And sometimes, we have confused the patience of God with the permission of God.
But Jesus never needed to approve of someone's sin to love them completely.
Think about that.
He could look directly into a person's brokenness without pretending their brokenness was harmless.
He could sit at a table with people considered morally unclean without becoming indifferent to holiness.
He could confront religious hypocrisy without abandoning righteousness.
He could speak truth without cruelty.
And He could offer mercy without surrendering truth.
That is not a contradiction.
That is the beauty of His character.
Consider Levi, the tax collector.
In the first-century Jewish world, tax collectors were often despised because of their association with Roman authority and the opportunities their occupation provided for exploitation.
When Jesus called Levi, He did not wait until Levi had built an impressive religious reputation.
He simply said:
“Follow me.” — Luke 5:27, KJV
And Levi rose and followed Him.
Soon afterward, Jesus was eating with tax collectors and others whom religious leaders regarded as sinners.
The Pharisees and scribes complained.
Why would someone claiming to represent God associate with people like these?
Jesus answered:
“They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” — Luke 5:31–32, KJV
Read that again.
Not merely sinners to dinner.
Not merely sinners to social acceptance.
Sinners to repentance.
But notice how He approached them.
He came near.
He shared a table.
He called them.
He offered them a new future.
Jesus did not require sinners to heal themselves before coming to the Physician.
Yet He did not come to tell the sick that their sickness needed no healing.
He came because they needed Him.
And so do we.
Imagine walking into a hospital with a wound that is slowly destroying your body.
The doctor examines you.
He sees the infection.
He knows the danger.
Then he smiles and says, “I accept you exactly as you are. There is nothing that needs to change.”
Would that be compassion?
Would that be love?
Not if he knew you were dying.
A loving physician does not humiliate the patient.
But neither does he pretend that the wound is healthy.
Jesus came as the Physician of souls.
His grace is not an excuse to remain spiritually sick.
It is the undeserved mercy through which sinners are brought to the One who heals.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Because it is easy to agree that Jesus should confront sin when the sin belongs to someone else.
It becomes uncomfortable when He touches ours.
We celebrate when He confronts greed.
Until He begins addressing our obsession with money.
We celebrate when He condemns hypocrisy.
Until He exposes the version of ourselves we perform in public.
We celebrate when He teaches forgiveness.
Until He asks us to release the bitterness we have carefully preserved for years.
We celebrate when He calls people to purity.
Until His words reach our private habits, our screens, our secret conversations, and the things we keep justifying.
We love the idea of surrender.
Until surrender requires something we do not want to release.
And suddenly, the question is no longer whether Jesus accepted sinners.
The question becomes whether we will allow the Savior who welcomes us to tell us the truth.
There is another encounter in Scripture that exposes how deeply Jesus understood this struggle.
A wealthy man approached Him, asking what he must do to inherit eternal life.
Mark's Gospel records an extraordinary detail.
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him.” — Mark 10:21, KJV
Jesus loved him.
Before the man made the sacrifice Jesus would ask of him.
Before he demonstrated obedience.
Before he walked away sorrowful.
Jesus loved him.
And what did Jesus do with that love?
He confronted the thing that held the man's heart.
Jesus instructed him to sell what he possessed, give to the poor, and follow Him.
The man went away grieving because he had great possessions.

Now, this passage does not mean that every Christian is commanded to sell everything they own. Jesus' specific instruction exposed the attachment that was preventing this particular man from following Him.
But the principle is painfully clear.
Jesus' love did not stop Him from making a costly demand.
He did not soften the call merely to keep the man comfortable.
And He did not redefine discipleship to make surrender unnecessary.
He loved the man enough to reveal what was standing between him and wholehearted allegiance to God.
Sometimes the most loving words Jesus speaks are the words that expose what is destroying us.
And sometimes the most heartbreaking response is to walk away because we would rather keep what enslaves us than surrender it to the One who can set us free.
There is a sentence that deserves to stay with us:
Jesus will receive the sinner who comes to Him, but receiving His grace is not the same as receiving His permission to continue in rebellion.
We see this clearly in another encounter, one with an unusually secure place in the Gospel narrative.
In Luke 19, Jesus met a man named Zacchaeus.
A chief tax collector.
Rich.
Despised.
A man whose profession placed him among the people many considered corrupt and unworthy of respectable company.
Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus.
But Jesus stopped beneath the branches.
Looked up.
And called him by name.
“Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house.” — Luke 19:5, KJV
Imagine that moment.
The crowd knew his reputation.
They knew the kind of man they believed him to be.
Yet Jesus chose to enter his home.
And the crowd complained that He had gone to be the guest of a sinner.
But something happened in that encounter.
Zacchaeus stood and declared that he would give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
Then Jesus said:
“This day is salvation come to this house.” — Luke 19:9, KJV
Do you see it?
Jesus did not wait for Zacchaeus to become respectable before drawing near to him.
But the encounter did not leave Zacchaeus clinging to his old way of life.
His repentance bore visible fruit.
The money that once represented his security became something he was willing to release.
The people he had wronged became people he was willing to repay.
The man who climbed a tree to see Jesus came down to a life that would never be the same.
That is what grace does.
Not always in a single dramatic moment.
Not always without struggle.
Not always without painful setbacks.
But genuine grace does not leave the human heart permanently indifferent to the will of God.
The apostle Paul explained this with striking clarity:
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
In Greek, Paul's forceful response begins:
μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito)
An emphatic rejection, commonly rendered “By no means!” in modern English translations.
Paul was confronting the idea that God's abundant grace gives believers a reason to continue in sin.
His answer was unmistakable.
No.
Grace is not a license for rebellion.
In Romans 6, Paul grounds this teaching in the believer's union with Christ in His death and resurrection.
Christians are called to walk in newness of life because they belong to the risen Savior.
And Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live in a godly manner.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace also teaches.
Grace reshapes.
Grace calls us out of the darkness we once defended.
But please hear this carefully.
That does not mean a genuine Christian will never struggle again.
It does not mean every temptation disappears the moment someone believes.
It does not mean that someone who falls has automatically been abandoned by God.
The Christian life involves ongoing repentance, dependence on the Holy Spirit, and growth in holiness.
The apostle John wrote to believers:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” — 1 John 1:8, KJV
And immediately afterward:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
So there is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
A difference between falling and deciding that you no longer need to rise.
A difference between crying out for deliverance and demanding that God call darkness light.
If you are struggling today, do not mistake the presence of a battle for proof that God has rejected you.
Bring the battle into the light.
Confess honestly.
Seek help when you need it.
Return to Christ.
Keep walking in repentance and faith.
And remember that forgiveness is not earned by how convincingly you hate yourself.
Forgiveness rests on Jesus Christ and His finished work.
But we must also address the other side of this conversation.
Because some people speak about repentance with a harshness that makes wounded sinners afraid to approach the Savior.
They know how to quote judgment.
They know how to identify moral failure.
They know how to tell people what is wrong with their lives.
But they seem to have forgotten how Jesus treated people who were broken, ashamed, and desperate for mercy.
Jesus was never indifferent to sin.
Yet some of His strongest rebukes were directed toward religious leaders whose outward righteousness concealed pride, hypocrisy, and a lack of mercy.
In Matthew 23, Jesus condemned religious hypocrisy.
In Luke 18:9–14, He told the parable of a Pharisee and a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood before God and praised himself for not being like other sinners.
The tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift his eyes toward heaven.
He prayed:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13, KJV
And Jesus said it was the tax collector who went home justified rather than the self-exalting Pharisee.
That should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Because it is possible to defend biblical morality while quietly becoming proud of our own supposed superiority.
It is possible to condemn another person's visible sin while protecting our own hidden arrogance.
It is possible to speak the language of holiness while forgetting our absolute dependence on mercy.
And it is possible to be so preoccupied with winning arguments about Jesus that we stop resembling Him in the way we treat people.
The cross leaves no room for spiritual boasting.
Every redeemed person stands there because of grace.
Not because their past was cleaner.
Not because their temptations were easier.
Not because their sins were more socially acceptable.
But because Jesus Christ is a merciful Savior.
This is why we must never confuse repentance with public humiliation.
Biblical repentance is not a performance staged to satisfy religious spectators.
It is a sincere turning to God.
And Christians are called to restore those caught in transgression with gentleness, while watching themselves lest they too be tempted (Galatians 6:1).
Truth without love can become cruelty.
Love without truth can become deception.
But in Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet perfectly.
John 1:14 says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.
The Greek words are:
χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (charitos kai alētheias)
Grace and truth.
Not grace instead of truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And that is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to either of the slogans we often hear.
“Jesus accepts everyone, so nobody needs to change.”
That is not the message Jesus preached.
“Jesus only accepts people after they have cleaned up their lives.”
That is not the message Jesus preached either.
The biblical picture is richer, more demanding, and infinitely more hopeful.
Jesus invites sinners to come to Him.
He commands people everywhere to repent.
He receives those who come to Him in faith.
He forgives through His saving work.
And He calls His followers into a transformed life.
His welcome is real.
His holiness is real.
His mercy is real.
His authority is real.
And His power to change lives is real.
Listen to His promise:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
What extraordinary words.
The sinner who comes to Jesus is not met with a Savior who delights in turning away the repentant.
He is met by the One who came to save.
But that promise is not a declaration that every person is automatically saved regardless of repentance or faith.
Jesus also warned:
“Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.” — Luke 13:3, KJV
Both statements came from Jesus.
We do not honor Him by embracing one and erasing the other.
His invitation must not be silenced by our severity.
His warning must not be silenced by our desire for approval.
And perhaps that is the real scandal of grace.
Not that God pretends sin does not matter.
But that the holy God, against whom we have sinned, has made a way for sinners to be forgiven through the death and resurrection of His Son.
Think about the cross.
The hands that touched lepers were pierced.
The feet that walked toward the rejected were nailed.
The One who called sinners to repentance willingly suffered for sinners.
He was not crucified because sin was insignificant.
He was crucified because our need for redemption was that serious—and His love that great.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had perfected our behavior.
Not after we had repaired every relationship.
Not after we had become worthy of salvation.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
And He rose again.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and was raised from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed.
Salvation is not a prize for religious achievement.
It is God's gift of grace, received through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the very next verse teaches that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
The order matters.
We are not saved because our good works purchase God's approval.
We are saved by grace, and that grace produces a new life.
The fruit does not purchase the tree.
It reveals the life growing within it.
And now, perhaps, we have reached the part of this article that cannot remain theoretical.
Because there may be something you have been hiding.
Something you have been defending.
Something you have been calling a weakness when, deep inside, you know you have been refusing to surrender it.
Perhaps it is resentment.
Perhaps it is dishonesty.
Perhaps it is sexual sin.
Perhaps it is pride.
Perhaps it is an addiction.
Perhaps it is a relationship that keeps pulling you away from obedience to Christ.
Perhaps it is not some scandal visible to the world.
Perhaps it is simply the slow, quiet hardening of a heart that once loved Jesus more deeply than it does today.
And maybe you are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of promising.
Tired of smiling in front of people while privately wondering how you drifted so far from the person you once wanted to become.
If that is you, please understand this.
Jesus is not calling you to manufacture a spotless history before coming to Him.
He is calling you to come.
Not with excuses.
Not with carefully edited confessions.
Not with a rehearsed explanation for why everyone else is to blame.
Come honestly.
Come humbly.
Come believing that the Savior who exposes sin is also the Savior who forgives sinners.
You do not have to convince Jesus that your sin is harmless.
You can admit that it is serious.
And still find mercy in Him.
You do not have to pretend your past never happened.
You can bring it into the light.
And trust that His grace is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
You do not have to claim that you will never stumble again.
You can surrender today.
And depend on Him for tomorrow.
That is the difference between condemnation that drives a person into hopelessness and godly sorrow that leads toward repentance.
Second Corinthians 7:10 teaches that godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation.
God does not call you to despair over your sin as though Jesus were powerless to save.
He calls you to turn to the Savior who has overcome sin and death.
And if you are reading this while thinking of someone who has hurt you, disappointed you, or wandered far from God, remember something equally important.
You cannot repent on their behalf.
You cannot force them to love Jesus.
You cannot shame them into genuine faith.
But you can speak truth.
You can pray.
You can set wise boundaries.
You can refuse to call evil good.
And you can remember that the person standing before you is still someone who needs the mercy of Christ.
Do not make peace with sin.
But do not make an enemy of the sinner you are called to love.
Remember who you were before grace found you.
Remember how patient God has been with you.
Remember that the Savior who changed Zacchaeus, restored Peter, and showed mercy to Paul is still able to transform human lives.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Three times.
At the very moment when his courage mattered most, fear overcame him.
Yet after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
But his story did not end in the courtyard of denial.
Grace met him on the other side of failure.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else.
Your worst moment does not have to become the final chapter of your life.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
But it does not have to determine your future.
Your sin must be confessed, not celebrated.
Your brokenness must be brought to Christ, not hidden behind a religious performance.
And your hope must rest in Jesus, not in your ability to rewrite yesterday.
Because you cannot go back and erase what happened.
But through Christ, you can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That is not a promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
Some wounds take time to heal.
Some relationships require rebuilding trust.
Some wrongs demand restitution.
Some battles require accountability, wise counsel, and sustained obedience.
But none of those realities cancels the promise of new life in Christ.
God's grace is not superficial.
It reaches deeper than the reputation people remember.
Deeper than the failure you regret.
Deeper than the shame that keeps whispering that you are beyond redemption.
And it calls you into a life where Jesus, not your past, becomes your Lord.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending they have never fallen.
Not to entertain religious audiences with comforting words that never challenge the heart.
Not to make Christianity more fashionable by removing the cross, repentance, or holiness.
But to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ.
To the truth that convicts.
To the grace that restores.
To the Scriptures that nourish faith.
To the Gospel that transforms.
Because there are people scrolling through Facebook right now who are one honest encounter with biblical truth away from finally admitting they need the Savior.
There are fathers quietly carrying guilt.
Mothers praying for children who have wandered.
Young people confused by competing voices about identity, purpose, truth, and love.
Believers fighting temptations they are ashamed to confess.
People wounded by religious hypocrisy who have never been shown the beauty of Jesus Himself.
And people who have heard that God loves them but have never understood why Christ calls them to repentance.
They need more than inspirational sentences.
They need the Word of God.
They need sound teaching.
They need encouragement grounded in truth.
They need to know that grace is available, that repentance matters, and that Jesus Christ is worthy of their entire lives.
That is the mission we want to continue and expand.
And if this message has strengthened your faith, there is a meaningful way you can help carry that mission forward.
Not because God measures your devotion by a payment.
Not because your salvation, forgiveness, or standing before Christ depends on supporting a Facebook ministry.
And no human ministry should ever tell you otherwise.
But because freely choosing to support faithful Gospel work can be a genuine act of Christian generosity and stewardship.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers may share good things with those who teach them the Word (Galatians 6:6).
Second Corinthians 9:7 also reminds us that giving should not arise from pressure or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
If you believe in this mission, if these messages have helped you grow, and if you are financially able, consider making Gospel Warrior part of your regular Christian giving.
We honor that.
But it can be a beautiful expression of partnership in the Gospel.
And that partnership matters.
Because behind every article is the possibility of someone encountering a truth they desperately needed.
Behind every shared devotional may be a person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Behind every Christ-centered message may be a reader who finally realizes that Jesus is not inviting them to hide their sin, but to surrender it.
It is helping biblical encouragement and discipleship reach people who need it.
We want the Word of God to remain accessible.
We want new believers to have resources for spiritual growth.
We want struggling Christians to find sound encouragement.
We want families, seekers, and people rediscovering their faith to encounter the truth of Scripture.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your voluntary support matters.
And your willingness to share the Gospel matters.
Not merely because it helps a page grow.
But because someone in your circle may be living with a dangerous misunderstanding of Jesus.
Someone may believe they are too sinful to come to Him.
Someone else may believe His grace means repentance is unnecessary.
And someone may have spent years believing that Christianity is nothing more than religious people condemning everyone else.
This message might help them see something different.
A Savior who welcomes sinners.
A Lord who calls them to repentance.
A Redeemer who forgives.
A King who transforms.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has stopped going to church.
Invite the believer who has become spiritually exhausted.
Invite the person who is curious about Christianity but has never truly understood the Gospel.
Even invite someone who does not yet believe.
Not so we can win an argument.
But so they can encounter the message of Jesus Christ and examine the Scriptures for themselves.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not about the sins of the culture.
Not about the failures of the church.
Not about what someone else needs to repent of.
About you.
When was the last time you allowed the Word of God to confront something in your own life without immediately defending yourself?
When was the last time you prayed, not merely “Lord, bless my plans,” but “Lord, search my heart”?
When was the last time you stopped asking God to remove the consequences of a choice and started asking Him to transform the desires behind it?
When was the last time you came to Jesus with no performance, no excuses, and no attempt to appear more righteous than you are?
Maybe tonight is the night.
Maybe this is the moment to stop running.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is bringing something to your attention that you have avoided for a long time.
Do not harden your heart.
You do not need to make a public confession of private details in a Facebook comment.
But if you are ready to be honest before God, you can write:
Not to glorify your past, but to glorify the Savior who met you there.
Your honest words may encourage someone who thinks they are the only person still struggling.
Your testimony may remind someone that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is the turning of the heart toward the One in whom hope is found.
And if you do not know how to pray, perhaps begin here.
Lord Jesus, I have spent too much time trying to make You fit the version of faith that feels comfortable to me.
I have wanted Your mercy without always wanting Your correction.
I have sometimes judged the sins of others while hiding my own.
I have confused Your patience with approval, and sometimes I have allowed shame to convince me that Your forgiveness could never reach me.
But today, I want the truth.
Not a softer Gospel.
Not a crueler Gospel.
Your Gospel.
Show me what I need to surrender.
Give me a repentant heart.
Teach me to trust what You accomplished through Your death and resurrection.
Forgive me.
Restore me.
Make me more like You.
And help me show others the same grace and truth You have shown me.
Amen.
Now return with me to the question we began with.
Did Jesus accept everyone?
Or did He call everyone to repent?
He welcomed people others rejected.
He ate with sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He showed compassion to the ashamed.
He invited the weary to come to Him.
And He proclaimed repentance.
He warned of judgment.
He commanded people to follow Him.
He called for a faith that bears fruit.
He never taught that every person is automatically saved simply because He loves the world.
And He never taught that sinners must earn His invitation by becoming righteous before approaching Him.
The answer is not that we must choose between His compassion and His holiness.
The answer is that we must receive Jesus as He reveals Himself in Scripture.
The Savior who welcomes sinners is the Lord who calls sinners to repent.
The One who forgives is the One who transforms.
The One who died for us is the One who calls us to follow Him.
And the One who rose from the grave is powerful enough to give new life to people who thought their story was already over.
So do not use grace to defend the chains Christ came to break.
And do not use truth as a stone against people Christ calls you to love.
Come to Jesus.
Bring your failures.
Bring your shame.
Bring your questions.
Bring your wounded heart.
But come willing to surrender.
Because the greatest evidence of His love is not that He leaves us untouched by His holiness.
It is that He gave Himself to redeem us from sin and bring us into new life.
And that is why our message will remain the same, no matter how loudly the world demands something easier.
We will preach repentance without abandoning compassion.
We will proclaim grace without excusing sin.
We will speak truth without forgetting mercy.
We will point the ashamed toward forgiveness, the proud toward humility, the weary toward Christ, and the wandering toward home.
We will keep sharing the Gospel.
And by God's grace, we will keep reminding people that no scandal, no failure, and no ruined reputation is greater than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
Because the miracle of grace is not that Jesus looks at your chains and calls them freedom—it is that He loves you enough to break them.
